queries: axolotl limb regeneration body size rate

rows.measured: Adult axolotls regrow amputated limbs; making them metamorphose with thyroxine cut the limb regrowth rate twofold and caused carpal and digit malformations, while body size did not change the rate (age-matched adults). The paper gives a rate ratio, not days to full regrowth; no days-to-full-limb number was found in the abstracts opened.
rows.cite: Monaghan, James R., Adrian C. Stier, Francois Michonneau, et al. "Experimentally Induced Metamorphosis in Axolotls Reduces Regenerative Rate and Fidelity." *Regeneration (Oxford, England)* 1, no. 1 (2014): 2-14. https://doi.org/10.1002/reg2.8. PMID 27499857.

queries: Poss KD[Author] AND Science[journal] AND heart regeneration

rows.measured: Adult zebrafish fully regenerated the heart within 2 months after 20% of the ventricle was cut away (histology), with no lasting scar.
rows.cite: Poss, Kenneth D., Lindsay G. Wilson, and Mark T. Keating. "Heart Regeneration in Zebrafish." *Science* 298, no. 5601 (2002): 2188-90. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1077857. PMID 12481136.
rows.molecule: yes, but only as a requirement: fish with mutations in the mitotic checkpoint kinase Mps1 (gene ttk) failed to regenerate and formed scars. Mps1 is a general cell-division kinase, so it is needed for regrowth, not shown to be what makes the fish differ from mammals. UniProt Q8AYG3 (Danio rerio Ttk/Mps1, reviewed); human ortholog TTK P33981 (reviewed); both read 2026-10-19
rows.human: no; not found. No paper testing the zebrafish factor in a human cell was opened.
rows.drug: no; none found, no agency page opened
rows.T: T1=1 one gene; T2=0 intracellular kinase; T3=1 catalytic; T4=1 TTK is conserved from fish to human; T5=0 a large multi-domain kinase; T6=0 needed for cell division, not shown to be enough for regeneration. T=3

rows.measured: After a complete spinal cord cut, ctgfa mutant zebrafish formed about 71% less glial bridge across the lesion than wild-type siblings at 4 weeks post-injury and showed no swim recovery between 2 and 6 weeks, while wild-type fish recover (full text, PMC5114142).
rows.cite: Mokalled, Mayssa H., Chinmoy Patra, Amy L. Dickson, Toyokazu Endo, Didier Y. R. Stainier, and Kenneth D. Poss. rows.molecule: yes; connective tissue growth factor a (ctgfa, CCN2a), secreted; its C-terminal part carries the effect. UniProt Q5RI33 (Danio rerio ccn2a/ctgfa, unreviewed); human CCN2/CTGF P29279 (reviewed); both read 2026-10-19
rows.human: partial; human recombinant CTGF protein placed at the zebrafish lesion gave more than 10-fold more glial bridging at 1 week and better swimming by 2 weeks (same paper). That is a human protein in a fish, not a human cell or human assay; a human-cell test was not found.

queries: zebrafish photoreceptor regeneration light lesion Muller glia

rows.measured: In adult albino zebrafish given 7 days of constant 8000 lux light, rods and cones died by apoptosis within 24 h; rods and green, blue and UV cones were all replaced within the 28-day recovery, though the cone mosaic was not restored. Dividing cells next to Mueller glia supplied the new cells.

rows.measured: Spiny mice survived a single intratracheal bleomycin dose of 15 U/kg, five times the 3 U/kg dose that gave C57BL/6 mice lung fibrosis (5 and 15 U/kg are sub-lethal or lethal for C57BL/6). At 3 U/kg, lung collagen area about doubled in C57BL/6 at day 28 but did not rise in Acomys. Small groups, n = 3 to 4 per dose (full text, PMC12395645).
rows.cite: Basalova, Nataliya A., Vladimir S. Popov, Yulia G. Antropova, et al. "Acomys cahirinus Develop Lung Stroma Distortion but Not Fibrosis after Bleomycin-Induced Injury." *Inflammation and Regeneration* 45, no. 1 (2025): 27. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41232-025-00391-4. PMID 40883787.

rows.species: Loxodonta africana (TP53 copy count); the cancer mortality is from zoo necropsy data on elephants, n = 644, African and Asian not split in the abstract
rows.measured: Estimated cancer mortality in elephants 4.81% (95% CI 3.14%-6.49%), against 11% to 25% in humans, despite their size and life span.
rows.cite: Abegglen, Lisa M., Aleah F. Caulin, Ashley Chan, et al. "Potential Mechanisms for Cancer Resistance in Elephants and Comparative Cellular Response to DNA Damage in Humans." *JAMA* 314, no. 17 (2015): 1850-60. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2015.13134. PMID 26447779.
rows.origins: One lineage for this route: the TP53 copy gain happened in the elephant (Proboscidean) lineage, at the same time as large body size evolved. Sulak, Michael, Lindsey Fong, Katelyn Mika, et al. "TP53 Copy Number Expansion Is Associated with the Evolution of Increased Body Size and an Enhanced DNA Damage Response in Elephants." *eLife* 5 (2016): e11994. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.11994. PMID 27642012. The number of separate origins of cancer resistance across large mammals was not found.
rows.molecule: yes; TP53, at least 20 copies in African elephants (40 alleles) against 1 in humans, including 19 retrogenes with transcription shown by RT-PCR (Abegglen 2015). UniProt lists 32 unreviewed 'Cellular tumor antigen p53' entries for Loxodonta africana (e.g. G3UI57); human TP53 P04637 (reviewed); read 2026-10-19
rows.human: partial; the same paper compared elephant and human blood lymphocytes side by side: after ionizing radiation 14.64% of elephant cells died by p53-driven apoptosis against 7.17% of human control cells and 2.71% of Li-Fraumeni cells. That is elephant cells next to human cells, not an elephant molecule acting in a human cell; such a test was not found.
